text: Unicode separates a code point from its encoding. Why is that separation useful?
choices: It keeps the character set small enough to fit in 16 bits, with encodings handling the rest.
It lets the character set be defined once and stored several ways, so a new encoding does not require renumbering every character.
It permits variable-length encodings, which fixed code points would otherwise forbid.
It allows the same code point to mean different characters in different languages.
explanation: U+00E9 is é permanently and independently of storage; UTF-8 spends two bytes on it, UTF-16 spends two, UTF-32 spends four. That is the same abstraction move the rest of the book keeps making — separate what a thing *is* from how it is *represented* — and it is why UTF-8 could be invented in 1992, years after the character assignments, without disturbing them.
